title: Short-term AI literacy intervention does not reduce over-reliance on incorrect ChatGPT recommendations
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether a very short AI literacy intervention can reduce high school students’ over-reliance on incorrect recommendations from ChatGPT. The core problem is that students may accept plausible but wrong large language model outputs without sufficient verification, which could undermine critical thinking and decision making. The authors focus specifically on whether a brief educational text about how ChatGPT works, its limitations, and tips for wise use can reduce this tendency.

The study used an experimental design in which 12th-grade Estonian high school students were randomly assigned to either an intervention group or a control group. The intervention group read a short AI literacy text covering ChatGPT’s working mechanism, limitations and risks, and usage guidance; the control group read only a shorter general introduction to ChatGPT. Students then completed eight math puzzles on an online survey platform while viewing screenshots of ChatGPT recommendations, half of which were intentionally incorrect. The main outcomes were over-reliance (accepting incorrect AI advice), under-reliance (rejecting correct AI advice), self-reported perceived AI literacy gains, confidence, and decision time.

The participants were 36 final-sample 12th-grade students from 10 Estonian high schools, and the study was conducted online in October 2024. The intervention itself was extremely brief, averaging about 3.4 minutes of reading time beyond the control text. The educational context is secondary education rather than higher education, which the authors position as important because many prior over-reliance studies have used university students.

The main conclusion is that the short AI literacy intervention did not significantly reduce over-reliance on incorrect ChatGPT recommendations. Students still adopted incorrect suggestions at high rates overall, with mean over-reliance of 52.1%. The intervention did, however, significantly increase under-reliance, meaning students became more likely to ignore correct ChatGPT recommendations. Students in the intervention group reported greater perceived knowledge about how ChatGPT works and how to use it, but not significantly greater knowledge about its limitations. The authors conclude that over-reliance on ChatGPT is widespread among secondary students and is not easily reduced by a brief informational intervention.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized controlled K-12 experiment, which strengthens causal inference, but it has substantial concerns including a very small final sample (n=36), likely limited power, and use of researcher-created task measures in a narrow context. These issues keep it below blue tier.
impact_tier_rationale: The intervention did not improve the main targeted behavior and produced a statistically significant negative effect on under-reliance toward correct ChatGPT recommendations (d=0.78 in the undesirable direction). Overall impact is therefore best classified as no impact or negative impact.

interventions.use_case: High school students solved math puzzles while receiving ChatGPT recommendations, with the study testing whether a short AI-literacy text changes students’ reliance on correct versus incorrect LLM advice.

finding.finding_summary: In a randomized high-school experiment, students used ChatGPT recommendations while solving eight math puzzles (final n=36; intervention n=19, control n=17). Over-reliance on incorrect ChatGPT advice was high overall (52.1%, SD=28.90) and was not significantly reduced by the AI-literacy intervention, t(28.78)=-0.73, p=.236, d=-0.25; however, the intervention significantly increased under-reliance on correct ChatGPT recommendations (36.84% vs. 19.12%), t(34)=2.35, p=.025, d=0.78, suggesting worse uptake of correct support.
finding.measure: Rates of over-reliance and under-reliance while solving Kangaroo math puzzles with correct/incorrect ChatGPT recommendations
finding.effect_size: d=-0.25 for over-reliance; d=0.78 for under-reliance
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI reported in figure only; exact values not_reported
finding.std_deviation: Over-reliance SD=28.90 overall; intervention SD=24.26, control SD=33.69. Under-reliance SD=24.00 overall; intervention SD=24.11, control SD=20.78

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively studies critical evaluation of AI outputs and over-reliance as a durable-skill issue. Students adopted at least one incorrect ChatGPT recommendation in 94.4% of cases, and longer decision time was associated with less over-reliance (rs=-0.41, p=.013), while the intervention itself did not improve deliberation and appears insufficient to reduce uncritical acceptance of AI output.
finding.measure: Over-reliance on incorrect AI recommendations, initial decision time, and critical evaluation of AI outputs
finding.effect_size: rs=-0.41 for over-reliance with incorrect-item decision time; rs=0.35 for under-reliance with correct-item decision time

finding.finding_summary: Students in the intervention group reported higher perceived knowledge about ChatGPT usage and working mechanism, but not limitations, after reading the educational text. Specifically, self-reported knowledge increased for usage, t(34)=2.26, p=.030, d=0.76, and working mechanism, t(34)=2.09, p=.044, d=0.70, while confidence in puzzle answers did not differ significantly between groups (U=188.50, p=.400, rrb=0.17).
finding.measure: Self-reported AI-literacy perceptions and self-perceived confidence in answers
finding.effect_size: d=0.76 (usage), d=0.70 (working mechanism), d=0.19 (limitations, non-significant), rrb=0.17 (confidence, non-significant)
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI reported in figures only; exact values not_reported
finding.std_deviation: Usage SD=0.77 vs 0.97; working mechanism SD=0.76 vs 0.90; limitations SD=0.91 vs 1.03; confidence SD=0.46 vs 0.76
